P00AE.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 for bank 2 measures the intake air temperature in the second intake path, typically near the air filter or in the air flow meter of that bank, on engines with two separate intake paths. For P00AE, the signal jumps faster than a real temperature can change, which typically points to a loose contact. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. Bank 2 codes occur only on engines with two separate intake or charge-air paths, one per cylinder bank.

causes.label: Loose contact or wire broken by movement
Sensor failing intermittently
Interference on the signal wire

symptoms: Emissions test or readiness check may fail

P00AF.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance
P00AF.description: Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger.

causes.label: Electronics or motor inside the actuator faulty
Sector gear or vane mechanism sticking (soot, coking), causing overcurrent
Weak supply or ground, corroded connector
Software of actuator or control module

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost
Often stored with actuator position or boost codes

P00B0.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Module Performance
P00B0.description: Boost control B here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. B denotes the second, separate actuator. P00B0 is set when actuator B reports an internal fault. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Electronics or motor inside the actuator faulty
Sector gear or vane mechanism sticking (soot, coking), causing overcurrent
Weak supply or ground, corroded connector
Software of actuator or control module

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost

P00B1.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit
P00B1.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B1 is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.

causes.label: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position)
Sensor faulty
Loose contact in the circuit
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended

P00B2.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P00B2.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B2 is a plausibility or range fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example because it is stuck at one value. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the exact logic is manufacturer-specific.

causes.label: Sensor drifting
Air at the sensor or low coolant level
Contact resistance at the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended

P00B3.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P00B3.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B3 means the sensor resistance or signal voltage is very low, typically a short to ground; with an NTC sensor the control module then reads an extremely high temperature (around 150 °C in a documented case).

causes.label: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position)
Sensor shorted internally
Signal wire shorted to ground
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended

P00B4.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P00B4.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B4 means the sensor resistance or signal voltage is very high, typically an open circuit or a short to the reference voltage; with an NTC sensor the control module then reads an extremely low temperature (around −60 °C in a documented case).

causes.label: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position)
Sensor open internally
Signal wire broken or shorted to reference or battery voltage
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended

P00B5.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P00B5.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B5 is set when the signal jumps or drops out briefly, which typically points to a loose contact. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.

causes.label: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position)
Sensor faulty
Loose contact in the circuit
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended

P00B6.title: Radiator Coolant Temperature/Engine Coolant Temperature Correlation
P00B6.description: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. After a long standstill (eight hours in a documented case) engine and radiator should be at the same temperature. P00B6 is set at the next start when the engine and radiator coolant temperature sensors differ by more than a threshold that may depend on intake air temperature. A detected engine block heater cancels the test. From this alone the control module cannot tell which sensor is wrong.

causes.label: Radiator coolant temperature sensor drifting
Engine coolant temperature sensor drifting
Contact resistance at a connector
Retrofitted engine preheater or auxiliary heater not detected by the system

P00B7.title: Engine Coolant Flow Low/Performance
P00B7.description: When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator. The usual cause is a thermostat stuck closed; low coolant, air in the system, a pump that delivers too little or a blocked radiator have the same effect. If the temperature keeps rising, stop driving to avoid engine damage.

causes.label: Thermostat stuck closed
Low coolant level or air in the cooling system
Coolant pump delivering too little (impeller, drive; known cases on some engines)
Radiator or hoses blocked
One of the temperature sensors reading wrong

symptoms: High engine temperature up to overheating

P00B8.title: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2
P00B8.description: On engines with two intake paths, the control module compares the manifold pressure of bank 2 with the measured or calculated air quantity of that bank. P00B8 is set when the two do not fit together; the code does not say which value is wrong. As with its bank 1 counterpart, typical causes are an air leak, an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close, or a dirty or drifting sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Air leak in the intake of bank 2
EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Manifold pressure sensor or air flow meter dirty or drifting
Wiring or connector faulty

P00B9.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature
P00B9.description: This code reports too low a pressure in the low-pressure fuel supply between the lift pump and the high-pressure pump under the additional condition of low ambient temperature. It separates cold-related supply problems from the general case. A typical mechanism, documented for diesel engines, is wax separating from insufficiently winterised fuel at sub-zero temperatures and clogging the filter or tank strainer. No manufacturer description naming this exact code, its thresholds or the vehicles using it was found.

causes.label: Wax separation from summer or insufficiently winterised diesel in frost
Fuel filter clogged or water in the filter frozen
Fuel filter heater faulty
Lift pump weak

symptoms: Jerking or loss of power after starting

P00BA.title: Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power
P00BA.description: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BA: power has been limited because fuel pressure is too low, which protects the engine and the pump against running lean or losing rail pressure.

causes.label: Fuel filter clogged, suction-side leak or air in the system
Lift pump or high-pressure pump weak
Pressure regulator or relief valve leaking
Tank run empty
Pressure sensor faulty

symptoms: Marked loss of power, limp mode

P00BB.title: Fuel Injector Insufficient Flow - Forced Limited Power
P00BB.description: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BB: power has been limited because the injectors do not deliver enough fuel, for example due to coking or wear; low rail pressure or missing injector coding after a replacement have a similar effect.

causes.label: Injectors coked or worn (flow drift)
Fuel contamination
Rail pressure too low
Injector coding missing after replacement

symptoms: Marked loss of power, limp mode

P00BC.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low
P00BC.description: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BC concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Air leak behind the meter or charge-air leak
Air flow meter dirty
Air filter or intake restricted
Wiring or connector faulty

P00BD.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too High
P00BD.description: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BD concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are a drifting or oil-coated meter or a wrong model value, for example from a faulty manifold pressure sensor or an open exhaust gas recirculation valve. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Air flow meter drifting or oil-coated
Model value wrong, e.g. faulty manifold pressure sensor or EGR valve stuck open
Leak upstream of the meter causing pulsations

P00BE.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow B Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low
P00BE.description: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BE concerns air flow meter B, i.e. a second meter, for example in the second intake path of a V engine. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Air leak behind the meter or charge-air leak
Air flow meter dirty
Air filter or intake restricted
Wiring or connector faulty

P00BF.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow B Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too High
P00BF.description: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BF concerns air flow meter B, i.e. a second meter, for example in the second intake path of a V engine. Typical causes are a drifting or oil-coated meter or a wrong model value, for example from a faulty manifold pressure sensor or an open exhaust gas recirculation valve. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Air flow meter drifting or oil-coated
Model value wrong, e.g. faulty manifold pressure sensor or EGR valve stuck open
Leak upstream of the meter causing pulsations

P00C0.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit
P00C0.description: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C0 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously.

causes.label: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Valve coil open or shorted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P00C1.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P00C1.description: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C1 reports too low a voltage, typically a short to ground in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously.

causes.label: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Valve coil open or shorted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P00C2.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P00C2.description: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C2 reports too high a voltage, typically a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously.

causes.label: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Valve coil open or shorted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P00C3.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Range/Performance
P00C3.description: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. With P00C3 the circuit is electrically intact, but the valve does not behave as commanded, for example because it sticks or its position feedback is implausible. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Valve sticking or coked
Diaphragm or piston worn
Position feedback implausible

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P00C4.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B - Mechanical
P00C4.description: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C4 reports that the valve stays mechanically closed. A documented method detects this on overrun from the pulsation of the measured air mass that compressor surge causes when the valve should open.

causes.label: Valve stuck closed or coked
Diaphragm or piston worn
Valve not actuated correctly
Consequence of a boost or air flow fault

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P00C5.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Turbine Overspeed
P00C5.description: The control module has detected that turbocharger B runs above its permitted maximum speed. Speed is measured by a dedicated sensor per turbocharger where fitted, or estimated from a model of pressure ratio and air mass. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in series systems or the one on bank 2 in parallel systems. Typical causes are sticking boost control of this turbocharger or a charge-air leak; find the cause before driving on, as overspeed can destroy the turbocharger. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

causes.label: Boost control of turbocharger B sticking (wastegate or vanes)
Leak on the pressure side making the turbocharger work harder
Speed sensor or its wiring delivering wrong values
Operation at high altitude or software

P00C6.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking
P00C6.description: Direct-injection engines release injection only once the rail has reached a minimum pressure. P00C6 is set when this pressure is not reached quickly enough while cranking, or, in another documented variant, when it drops below the minimum again right after the high-pressure start. Cranking then takes longer or the engine does not start. The check runs once per start; some manufacturers only enable it above a minimum tank level.

causes.label: High-pressure pump weak, or its drive cam or follower worn
Lift pump or low-pressure supply too weak
Control valve on the pump faulty
Leak or check valve fault letting pressure bleed off after shutdown
Very low fuel level

P00C7.title: Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00C7.description: With the engine stopped, all pressure sensors in the intake system (manifold pressure, boost pressure, barometric pressure) should read ambient pressure; some diesels also compare them at idle. The control module compares them: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own code. P00C7 is set when the readings disagree but no single sensor can be identified as faulty, which points to a fault affecting several sensors, such as a shared reference voltage or ground.

causes.label: Shared 5 V reference or ground of the pressure sensors disturbed
Two sensors drifting at the same time (contamination, oil mist, ageing)
Pressure hose to a sensor leaking or blocked
Engine control module or software

symptoms: Substitute values with loss of power possible

P00C8.title: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
P00C8.description: Some engine control modules switch the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator A on both sides: the ground side is monitored by P0090 to P0092, the supply side (high-side driver) by P00C8 to P00CA. On gasoline direct injection the regulator is typically the control valve on the high-pressure pump. P00C8 reports an open circuit on the supply side. Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power.

causes.label: Supply wire or connector to the pump solenoid damaged by heat or chafing
Solenoid coil open
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00C9.title: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit Low
P00C9.description: Some engine control modules switch the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator A on both sides: the ground side is monitored by P0090 to P0092, the supply side (high-side driver) by P00C8 to P00CA. On gasoline direct injection the regulator is typically the control valve on the high-pressure pump; on some diesels it is the regulator designated as regulator 1. P00C9 reports a short to ground on the supply side. Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power; documented systems turn on the warning light in the first drive cycle.

causes.label: Supply wire to the solenoid chafed and shorted to ground
Solenoid coil shorted
Water or corrosion in the connector
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CA.title: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit High
P00CA.description: Some engine control modules switch the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator A on both sides: the ground side is monitored by P0090 to P0092, the supply side (high-side driver) by P00C8 to P00CA. On gasoline direct injection the regulator is typically the control valve on the high-pressure pump; on some diesels it is the regulator designated as regulator 1. P00CA reports a short to battery voltage on the supply side, so the driver can no longer switch the supply off. Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power; documented systems turn on the warning light in the first drive cycle.

causes.label: Supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Water or corrosion in the connector
Internal fault in the solenoid
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CB.title: Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
P00CB.description: The fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve that meters how much fuel the high-pressure pump delivers (metering unit on diesels, pump control valve on some gasoline direct-injection engines). Many control modules switch such solenoids on both sides; P0001 to P0004 cover the control side, while these codes cover the supply side (high-side driver). P00CB reports an open circuit on the supply side. Rail pressure may then deviate, with reduced power or hard starting. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Supply wire broken or connector corroded
Regulator coil open or shorted (often built into the pump)
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CC.title: Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit Low
P00CC.description: The fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve that meters how much fuel the high-pressure pump delivers (metering unit on diesels, pump control valve on some gasoline direct-injection engines). Many control modules switch such solenoids on both sides; P0001 to P0004 cover the control side, while these codes cover the supply side (high-side driver). P00CC reports a short to ground on the supply side. Rail pressure may then deviate, with reduced power or hard starting. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Regulator coil open or shorted (often built into the pump)
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CD.title: Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit High
P00CD.description: The fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve that meters how much fuel the high-pressure pump delivers (metering unit on diesels, pump control valve on some gasoline direct-injection engines). Many control modules switch such solenoids on both sides; P0001 to P0004 cover the control side, while these codes cover the supply side (high-side driver). P00CD reports a short to battery voltage on the supply side. Rail pressure may then deviate, with reduced power or hard starting. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Regulator coil open or shorted (often built into the pump)
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CE.title: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00CE.description: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. Some vehicles also disable start-stop while this code is stored.

causes.label: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code
Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine
Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors
Engine control module or software

P00CF.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Correlation
P00CF.description: With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor A (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure. This code is set when it deviates from the barometric pressure sensor by more than a threshold; the code does not say which of the two is wrong. Manufacturers that publish their diagnostics run the same comparison under other codes. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Boost pressure sensor dirty, oil-coated or drifting
Barometric sensor drifting, also when inside the control module
Contact resistance at connector, ground or 5 V reference
Sensor port or hose leaking or blocked

symptoms: Reduced boost or limp mode possible

P00D0.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor B Correlation
P00D0.description: With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor B (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure. This code is set when it deviates from the barometric pressure sensor by more than a threshold; the code does not say which of the two is wrong. B denotes the second boost pressure sensor, for example on a second turbocharger. Manufacturers that publish their diagnostics run the same comparison under other codes. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Boost pressure sensor dirty, oil-coated or drifting
Barometric sensor drifting, also when inside the control module
Contact resistance at connector, ground or 5 V reference
Sensor port or hose leaking or blocked

symptoms: Reduced boost or limp mode possible

P00D1.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P00D1.description: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2.

causes.label: Heating element aged, resistance increased
Corrosion or contact resistance at connector or harness of the heater circuit
Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground
Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles)
Replacement sensor with a different heater

symptoms: Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

P00D2.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2
P00D2.description: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor behind the catalytic converter (sensor 2) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit.

causes.label: Heating element aged, resistance increased
Corrosion or contact resistance at connector or harness of the heater circuit
Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground
Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles)
Replacement sensor with a different heater

symptoms: Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

P00D3.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Sensor 1
P00D3.description: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 2. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. P00D4.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Sensor 2

P00D5.title: HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2

P00D7.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High
P00D7.description: Bypass valve A is the electric compressor recirculation valve, mounted close to the hot compressor and turbine housing. This code reports that its temperature is too high. How the temperature is detected is not described in published manufacturer documents; a documented principle for comparable turbocharger solenoids estimates the coil temperature from current, supply voltage and duty cycle and protects the coil by limiting or switching it off. P00DE.title: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P00DE.description: With indirect charge air cooling, a water-to-air charge air cooler cools the charge air; it sits in a separate low-temperature coolant circuit with an electric pump and its own radiator. The charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor A measures the coolant temperature of this circuit. The control module uses it to control the pump and to monitor cooling performance. P00E3.title: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open
P00E3.description: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

Actuator faulty (electric or vacuum)
Linkage or return spring broken
Heat exchanger temperature sensor faulty, simulating a stuck valve

P00E5.title: Intake Air Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation
P00E5.description: After a long standstill, intake air and fuel should be at about ambient temperature. P00E6.title: Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
P00E6.description: This is the bank 2 counterpart of the multiple pressure sensor check for engines with separate pressure measurement per bank, such as twin-turbo V engines. With the engine stopped, all intake pressure sensors should read ambient pressure. If one stands out, it gets its own code; this code is set when the readings disagree but no single sensor can be identified, which points to a fault affecting several sensors such as a shared reference voltage or ground. P00E7.title: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2

P00F9.description: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge. One manufacturer documents it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. P00F9 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible. In a documented case the cause was a sensor not seated properly and a connector not fully engaged; securing them solved it without parts.

causes.label: Connector loose or not fully engaged, or sensor not seated properly
Sensor oil-coated from turbocharger oil mist or characteristic drifted
Leak at the sensor flange or seal
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with boost limitation

P00FA.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P00FA.description: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge. One manufacturer documents it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. P00FA means the signal is below its valid range, typically an open circuit, a short to ground or a missing 5 V reference. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

causes.label: Connector loose or not fully engaged, or sensor not seated properly
Wire interrupted, short to ground or 5 V reference missing
Leak at the sensor flange or seal
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with boost limitation

P00FB.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P00FB.description: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FB means the signal voltage is above its valid range: typically a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor. It does not mean the boost really is too high – that would be P0234. The circuit is monitored continuously from key-on; comparable GM pressure sensors fail above 86–97 % of the reference for about 4 s. The engine then works with a substitute value and may limit boost. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Sensor faulty internally (oil mist, heat at compressor outlet)
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with boost limit

P00FC.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P00FC.description: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FC covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal that are each too brief for the low or high code, or changes faster than real pressure can move. Comparable intermittent monitors count range violations per drive cycle – Ford's MAP check, for example, sets after 25 events. The FCA case for the sibling code P00F9 was a sensor not fully seated with an unlatched connector, exactly the kind of fault that produces erratic signals; heat and vibration near the turbocharger add to it. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.

causes.label: Connector loose, not latched, or terminals corroded or spread
Harness chafed or broken near the turbocharger (heat, vibration)
Sensor with internal dropouts
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on, possibly only after several drives
Occasional hesitation or brief loss of power under load

P00FD.title: Battery B State of Charge Performance
P00FD.description: 'Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks. The engine module sets P00FD if the auxiliary battery is disconnected on the first start, drops below about 8 V during an auto-start, or repeatedly falls below 10.3 V (counter reaches ten). Start-stop is then disabled; often it follows a jump start or many short trips. Whether the MIL comes on is not stated in the sources.

causes.label: Auxiliary battery discharged or aged
Loose or corroded positive or ground connections at either battery
150 A fuse or fuse array in the power distribution centre open or poorly contacting
Battery separation relay stuck
Main battery faulty

symptoms: Start-stop out of service, 'Service Start/Stop' message
'Service Shifter' message with electronic gear selector

P00FE.title: EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
P00FE.description: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister.

causes.label: Kinked, pinched or misrouted vapour line between tank and canister
Charcoal canister broken down, grains blocking lines or valves
Rollover or fill-limit valve at the tank stuck closed (e.g. after overfilling)
Purge valve or leak detection module faulty
Tank pressure sensor reading wrong

symptoms: Fuel nozzle clicks off early when refuelling
Hiss or vacuum when opening the fuel cap

P00FF.title: Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P00FF.description: P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there. GM documents two cases – a 2020 Cadillac CT5 with climate flap actuator codes and 2025 full-size SUVs with U1962 – both cured by reprogramming the body control module, not by replacing parts. The mechanism matches other 'module requested MIL' codes such as P069E. P00FF itself causes no limp mode.

causes.label: Emissions-relevant fault in the body control module or its sensors/actuators (own B/U codes)
Software or calibration fault in the body control module
Communication fault on the data bus
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on without an engine fault
Other messages depending on the body module fault

P0100.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
P0100.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)
Supply fuse or relay failed
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)

P0101.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0101.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.

causes.label: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak)
Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust)
Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring

symptoms: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems
Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response
Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174

P0102.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
P0102.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value.

causes.label: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded or loose
Sensor electronics failed
Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay) or poor ground
Large leak or disconnected duct between sensor and throttle

symptoms: Lack of power, hesitation, substitute value mode

P0103.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit High
P0103.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0103 means the signal is above its electrical upper limit. Documented limits: GM petrol 14,500 Hz or more, GM diesel above 12,500 Hz, Saab 9-4X above about 15,150 Hz, Ford analogue above 4.785 V (checked only below 4,000 rpm so that high load is not mistaken for a fault). Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to a voltage source, failed sensor electronics or interference from a harness routed too close to ignition coils, relays or motors. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine switches to a calculated air mass.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the supply wire
Sensor electronics failed
Interference from harness routed near ignition coils, relays or motors
Water in the connector or on the element

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power

P0104.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0104.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0104 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal without a permanent low or high fault – the classic sign of a loose contact. In Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary the code is set once more than 25 short open or short-circuit events have been counted. GM and Saab do not list P0104 in the documents checked; there such dropouts end up under P0102/P0103 or P0101. The trip count is not stated by Ford. Diagnosis means moving the harness while watching the live signal and checking terminals for corrosion and weak tension.

causes.label: Loose contact at the sensor connector (corrosion, spread terminals, broken latch)
Chafed or partly broken wire moved by the engine
Sensor electronics dropping out (temperature-dependent)
Poor ground or electrical interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may go out again
Occasional hesitation, misfire-like stumble, flat spot

P0105.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit
P0105.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0105 is the general circuit fault and is rarely used today: most petrol engines report low, high and intermittent separately (P0107–P0109). It appears mainly where the fault cannot be broken down further – Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the digital SENT sensor reports a bad status or an out-of-limit value for 5 s (lost communication is a separate U code), and Bosch EDC16 diesels use it with a fault type byte, for example signal below 0.2 V. Saab then substitutes 101.3 kPa, limits torque and switches off EGR and boost control.

causes.label: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose
MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault)
Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)

P0106.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0106.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0106 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or drifting. Two tests are common. With the engine stopped, all pressures equalise, so MAP must match ambient (and boost) pressure; Ford allows 1.5–3 inHg. While running, MAP is compared with a value modelled from air mass, throttle and speed – GM blames the MAP sensor above about 23–30 kPa error, with two trips on petrol and one on diesel. Turbo engines with three sensors find the odd one out by majority. Besides the sensor, intake or boost leaks often cause it.

causes.label: Vacuum leak at the intake manifold or boost leak (hose, clamp, charge air cooler)
Sensor oiled or sooted, port blocked (EGR soot), characteristic drifted
High resistance in signal, reference or ground wire
Comparison sensor wrong, or mechanical cause (dirty throttle, EGR stuck open)

symptoms: Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0107.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P0107.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0107 means the signal voltage is below its lower limit. 'Low' refers to the voltage, not to a real low pressure: typically the signal wire is grounded, the signal or 5 V reference is open, or the sensor has failed. A short on another sensor sharing the same reference can pull it down too, so GM often sees several codes at once. Documented limits: GM below 3.3 % of 5 V (about 0.17 V), GM/Saab 2.0T below 0.19 V for 4 s, Ford petrol below 0.19 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.1 V. GM petrol needs two trips, GM diesel one. A modelled value replaces the reading.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing)
5 V reference shorted by another faulty sensor on the same circuit
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard starting, rough idle, stalling possible
Wrong mixture from substitute value, higher consumption
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo and diesel engines

P0108.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P0108.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0108 means the signal voltage is above its upper limit – typically an open ground (low reference), a signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, or a failed sensor. Like P0107 it describes the voltage, not real overpressure; genuinely excessive boost is P0234. Documented limits: GM petrol above 86 % of 5 V, GM diesel above 97 %, GM/Saab 2.0T above 4.80 V for 4 s, Ford above 4.88–4.96 V for 5 s. The engine substitutes a modelled value, which often makes the mixture too rich; turbo engines limit boost.

causes.label: Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0109.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0109.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0109 counts brief range violations of the signal that are too short for P0107/P0108 – the typical signature of a loose contact. Ford counts excursions below 0.024 V or above 4.96 V and sets the code after 25 events per drive cycle (2020–2023; ten in 2012). Ford treated it as a code without warning light in 2012 but lights the MIL in 2020–2023, so the warning-light behaviour depends on the manufacturer. GM does not use P0109 in the tables checked; there short dropouts accumulate in P0107/P0108.

causes.label: Loose contact at the MAP connector, terminals spread or corroded
Chafed or broken wire that makes contact with engine movement
Sensor with internal dropouts
Ground problem or control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)

P010A.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit
P010A.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary lists it for a broken element of digital sensor B, with the same limit as sensor A (period above 1.3 ms for half a second); which engines carry sensor B is not stated. GM's twin-turbo V6 only uses the other sensor B codes. The engine can run on values calculated from manifold pressure, throttle and the remaining sensor.

causes.label: Connector or wiring of sensor B open
Sensor B faulty internally (broken element)
Supply of sensor B missing (fuse, relay)
Control module input faulty

P010B.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P010B.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010B is the plausibility fault of sensor B: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. GM checks it like sensor A against a model built from the other sensors (manifold pressure, boost, throttle, sensor A) and fails it above 20 g/s deviation, with two trips. For the VR30DDTT Nissan names a loose or leaking left-hand intake pipe as the main cause and warns against touching or dismantling the sensor. Other causes match P0101: a soiled element, a clogged filter on that side or a boost leak.

causes.label: Intake pipe on the sensor B side leaking or not seated
Sensor B element contaminated (oil, dust)
Air filter on that side clogged or wrongly fitted
Boost leak on that bank, or sensor/connector problem

P010C.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Low
P010C.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010C means the signal of sensor B is below its electrical lower limit – the counterpart of P0102. GM's twin-turbo V6 sets it at 400 Hz or less (300 failed out of 375 samples, two trips); Ford's digital sensor B below 1.5 kHz for 5 s. The usual causes are an open or grounded signal wire, a corroded connector, missing supply or failed sensor electronics. The engine continues with a calculated substitute value.

causes.label: Signal wire of sensor B open or grounded, connector corroded
Sensor B electronics failed
Supply or ground of sensor B faulty
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Lack of power, substitute value mode

P010D.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit High
P010D.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010D means the signal of sensor B is above its electrical upper limit – the counterpart of P0103. GM's twin-turbo V6 sets it at 14,500 Hz or more (two trips); Ford's digital sensor B when the signal period drops below 83 microseconds, i.e. above roughly 12 kHz, for 5 s. Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to voltage, failed sensor electronics or interference from nearby ignition or actuator wiring. A substitute value is used.

causes.label: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to voltage
Sensor B electronics failed
Interference from harness routing
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power
Rich mixture and higher consumption possible

P010E.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P010E.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010E covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of sensor B without a lasting low or high fault, the counterpart of P0104. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary sets it after more than 25 short open or short-circuit events; GM's twin-turbo V6 does not use it, and Ford does not state the trip count. The usual cause is a loose contact at the connector or a chafed wire that opens as the engine moves.

causes.label: Loose contact at the sensor B connector
Chafed or partly broken wire
Sensor B electronics dropping out
Poor ground or interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may come and go

P010F.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation
P010F.description: Engines with two intake paths have two mass air flow sensors, A and B. On a symmetrical V engine both sides should draw about the same amount of air, so the readings can be compared with each other. P010F is set when both signals are electrically valid but differ by more than allowed; the code does not say which side is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code or its threshold was found: GM's twin-turbo V6 and Nissan's VR30DDTT assess each sensor separately against a model (P0101/P010B). The description therefore rests on the CARB requirement for plausibility checks and on component sources for engines with two sensors. Typical causes are a leaking intake pipe or a soiled sensor on one side.

causes.label: Air leak or loose intake pipe on one side
One of the two sensors contaminated or aged
Air filter on one side clogged or wrongly fitted
Turbocharger or boost problem on one bank
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

symptoms: Mixture codes for one bank (P0171/P0174) possible

P0110.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Bank 1
P0110.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0110 is the general circuit fault. With a conventional analogue sensor most manufacturers report low and high signals separately (P0112/P0113), so P0110 mainly appears in two cases: with digital (SENT) sensors that combine air mass and temperature, where it stands for lost communication or an implausible status (Ford diesel 2023, after about 5 s), and in some Bosch systems as a collective code whose fault type byte tells open circuit from short to ground. The control module then uses a substitute temperature; some systems also limit torque.

causes.label: Connector or wiring to the sensor open or corroded
Sensor or mass air flow sensor with built-in temperature sensor faulty
Sensor supply or ground disturbed
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Reduced power or torque limitation on some systems
Otherwise usually inconspicuous; cold start may be slightly worse

P0111.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P0111.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0111 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. The usual test runs at key-on after a long soak (Ford 6 h, GM 8 h): the intake air sensor is compared with other temperature sensors such as coolant, cylinder head, charge air cooler or IAT2, which should all read about the same. GM flags it above about 25 °C deviation, Ford above about 17 °C; Ford first confirms with a drive above 40 mph because sunshine can warm a sensor, and also sets P0111 if the air reads over 66 °C while driving. A detected block heater suspends the test. Two consecutive trips are needed.

causes.label: Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (ageing, oil from crankcase ventilation)
Contact resistance at connector or wiring distorts the reading
Comparison sensor (coolant, IAT2, charge air cooler) wrong
Undetected preheater, heat soak or sensor mounted near a heat source

symptoms: Slightly changed idle, power or cold start possible
Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P0112.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low Bank 1
P0112.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0112 means the signal is below its valid range. With an NTC sensor that points to a short to ground in the signal wire or an internally shorted sensor, and the control module would read an implausibly hot value (GM about 150 °C). Documented limits: Ford petrol below 0.244 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.10 V, GM below 62 ohms. The circuit is monitored continuously; GM needs two trips. Some systems then use the coolant temperature, capped at 40 °C, as a substitute and limit torque.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed insulation)
Sensor shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Retarded ignition, reduced power or torque limit on some systems

P0113.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1
P0113.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0113 means the signal is above its valid range. With an NTC sensor that is typically an open circuit – connector off, broken wire, open sensor or missing ground – or a short to a voltage source, and the module would read an extremely cold value (GM about −60 °C). Documented limits: Ford petrol above 4.96 V for 5 s, Ford diesel above 4.91 V, GM above about 127 kilohms. A classic cause is a sensor left unplugged after an air filter change; one manufacturer bulletin describes broken wires at the connector caused by harness tension. Monitoring is continuous, GM needs two trips.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or loose, or wire broken
Sensor open internally
Sensor return (ground) wire open
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Slightly richer mixture and higher consumption possible

P0114.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
P0114.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0114 covers an unsteady signal. Air temperature changes slowly, so rapid jumps point to the wiring rather than the air. Ford counts short excursions out of range that are each too brief for P0112/P0113 and sets the code after ten of them in one drive cycle. GM evaluates noise within the valid range: if the readings taken every 100 ms add up to more than 80 °C of movement within one second, in four of five seconds, the sample counts as failed. GM needs two trips. Typical culprit is a loose contact that opens with engine movement.

causes.label: Loose contact at the connector (corrosion, weak terminal tension)
Partly broken wire that opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal contact problem
Electrical interference or ground fault

symptoms: Occasional brief stumble or rough idle possible

P0115.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
P0115.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0115 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. Today it has largely been replaced by P0117, P0118 and P0119; GM and Ford do not set it in the tables checked. Older or individual systems still use it as a collective code, for example Saab Trionic T5 (1998). The circuit is monitored continuously; when it fails, the module uses a substitute value and many systems run the radiator fan permanently.

causes.label: Connector corroded or loose, terminal spread
Broken or chafed signal or ground wire
Sensor faulty internally (short, open, coolant inside)
Control module input or 5 V supply faulty

P0116.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
P0116.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0116 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but not believable. Most often it checks for a sensor stuck too warm. After a long soak (GM 8 h, Ford 6 h) coolant must be close to intake air temperature; GM fails it above about 19 °C difference without a detected block heater, Ford if it reads over 110 °C or sits at 79–110 °C. Ford diesels instead check whether coolant warms fast enough in frost. A sensor stuck warm suppresses cold-start enrichment and can defeat the thermostat monitor, which is why CARB requires this test. GM uses one or two trips depending on the engine.

causes.label: Sensor drifting and reading too warm (ageing, coolant ingress)
Corrosion or contact resistance in connector or wiring
Block heater or preheater not detected
Comparison sensor (intake air, ambient) wrong
Control module calibration

P0117.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
P0117.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0117 means the signal voltage is too low, so the sensor would report an implausibly hot engine (around 140–160 °C). Usual causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, coolant or moisture in the connector, or an internally shorted sensor. Limits: GM below 55 ohms, Ford petrol below 0.244 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.10 V, Mitsubishi below 0.1 V for 2 s. Mitsubishi then calculates with 80 °C; GM/Saab switch the radiator fan on and the A/C compressor off. GM needs two trips. On Ford engines with a head temperature sensor the equivalent is P1290.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing, pinched harness)
Sensor shorted internally or coolant inside the sensor
Moisture or coolant in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard cold start (no enrichment, engine reported hot)

P0118.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
P0118.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0118 means the signal voltage sits near the 5 V reference, so the sensor would report about −40 °C. Typical causes are an unplugged or corroded connector, a broken signal or sensor ground wire, an open sensor or a short to voltage. Limits: GM above 134 kilohms (only after 10 s running, so genuine cold is not misread), Ford petrol above 4.96 V for 5 s, Ford diesel above 4.91 V, GM/Saab below −39 °C for 4 s. Without a substitute strategy the mixture would be far too rich; GM/Saab run the fan and switch off the A/C. On Ford engines with a head temperature sensor the equivalent is P1289.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, contact open
Broken signal or sensor ground wire
Sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rich mixture, higher consumption, possibly black smoke or fuel smell

P0119.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0119.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. Coolant temperature can only change slowly because of the thermal mass involved. P0119 is set when the reading jumps faster than physically possible. GM calculates, every second, a window for the next valid value from the previous reading and a sensor time constant of 13 s; readings outside it in three of four samples count as a fault, monitored continuously over two trips. GM/Saab set it after more than 4 s of abrupt changes and then run the radiator fan. Typical causes are loose contacts or a harness chafing as the engine moves.

causes.label: Loose contact or corroded connector pins
Harness chafing that briefly grounds or opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal crack or contact fault
Air pockets at the sensor (poorly bled cooling system)

symptoms: Radiator fan switches on for no reason
Occasional rough running or idle fluctuation

P011A.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation
P011A.description: Some engines have two coolant temperature sensors that check each other. P011A is set when both are electrically fine but their readings differ more than a calibrated amount under conditions where they should agree. Mazda documents the code for the 2013–2016 CX-5 and 2014–2016 Mazda6: sensor 2 sits in the heater hose, and a clogged heater core keeps it noticeably colder, so P011A often comes with weak cabin heat although both sensors are good. Mazda's check is to compare both sensors with ambient temperature after an overnight soak and then the temperature difference across the heater hoses. A block heater used below 0 °C can also trigger it.

causes.label: Clogged heater core or restricted coolant flow at sensor 2
One of the two sensors drifting
Air in the cooling system or low coolant level
Block heater use in frost
Contact resistance at one sensor

P011B.title: Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation
P011B.description: After a long standstill the coolant and the intake air should both have settled close to ambient temperature. P011B compares the two sensors at start-up and is set when they disagree without either sensor showing a circuit fault. In the documented GM/Saab version the engine must have been off for more than 10 hours with no preheater detected; the fault counts if coolant reads at least 20 °C above intake air, or intake air at least 30 °C above coolant, and the coolant reading barely moves (2 °C or less) in the first 45 s. The code does not say which sensor is wrong – that has to be found by comparing both with the actual ambient temperature. Toyota resolved false settings on some 2015 V6 engines with new software. Ford and GM report the same idea under the individual sensor codes.

causes.label: Coolant temperature sensor stuck or drifting
Intake air temperature sensor drifting or heat-soaked
